source_note: Verified Collins et al. BMJ 2024;384:e074819 (PMC10772854) full text: 'the value of optimism corrected calibration slope can be used to adjust the model from any overfitting by applying it as shrinkage factor to the original regression coefficients' -- tied to the bootstrap (Box 2); no mention of a K-fold out-of-fold slope. Van Houwelingen & le Cessie, Stat Med 1990;9:1303 (PMID 2277880) abstract: cross-validation 'can produce adjusted predictors with improved performance', which backs a cross-validated shrinkage factor in general (their construction is leave-one-out style, not the (K-1)/K fold models used here). Steyerberg 2019 §13.2 is a book, not verified. Internal: MODEL_FAMILY_CONTRACT C9 / ridge.py:37-38 (WAVE_C6A_PLAN §5 ruling 7) restricts it to the unpenalized family because ridge shrinkage is 'not sourced' -- a sourcing decision, not a methods derivation.
note: Code matches the statement: stages/evaluation.py:_shrinkage offers it only for families whose updating includes 'shrinkage' (linear.py:151, LinearRegression/LogisticRegression without penalty); slope_of (decision_curve.py:368) takes the bootstrap's corrected slope, else the out-of-fold slope, and the sentence names which. The R test (and test_previews_wave2b::test_set_updating_shrinks_by_the_fits_slope_with_the_intercept_re_estimated, statsmodels) check the arithmetic only, not that shrinking improves calibration on new rows; no known-truth simulation. Two things outside the cited regime: the OOF fallback is not Collins's estimator, and no guard stops the offer when the slope exceeds 1 (then it expands coefficients, and the preview caption 'each risk moves toward the mean' is false). decisions.py:1781 comment says 'optimism-corrected' only, which understates the fallback.

corrected_statement: For the proportional-odds model, independent rows get Wald intervals from the inverse observed information (z reference); when rows repeat within units and G is at or above the unit floor (seal.min_groups, default 8), the table uses the CR1 sandwich over units' summed scores with the G/(G-1) factor on t(G-1) -- Cameron & Miller's stated minimum, which they say still over-rejects with few clusters -- and refuses intervals below the floor. The table's concern lines, shared with the linear family, wrongly describe these intervals as CR2 with Bell-McCaffrey degrees of freedom.
source_note: Verified Cameron & Miller 2015 (JHR; author PDF, text extracted): 'at a minimum one should use the T(G-1) distribution rather than the standard normal'; c = G/(G-1) is 'a simpler correction that is also used by Stata for extensions to nonlinear models'; 'Either choice usually lessens, but does not fully eliminate, the usual downwards bias in the CRVE'; 'Especially when there are few clusters it is better still to use bias-adjusted cluster-robust standard errors or to use a wild cluster bootstrap'; Stata itself uses normal critical values for nonlinear models. So the source backs CR1+t(G-1) as a floor, not as 'valid 95% intervals' at small G. The Wald case is standard ML theory (MASS::polr, statsmodels OrderedModel) and the repo reproduces polr's published housing fit.
note: Parity tests (statsmodels sandwich rescaled to Stata's ML factor; MASS::polr published SEs in ::test_2_reproduces_mass_polr_published_housing_fit) are independent references for the computation but no coverage simulation exists, so validity at small G is not checked. Contradiction found by running ordinal_table with G = 12 (venv/bin/python; note .venv lacks pydantic so the prescribed .venv pytest command cannot import the engine): caption says 'CR1 ... on t(11)' while ordinal.py:398 prepends inference._cluster_concerns, which says 'Intervals are cluster-robust ... (CR2, G = 12)' and 'the intervals use the CR2 small-sample correction with Bell-McCaffrey degrees of freedom'. The user is told two different methods for the same table. Also weaker than the linear family's CR2+BM for the same situation.

corrected_statement: Under the dietary lens, the app raises the 'energy carries the nutrient' noticing, graded 'act on it' (changes_question, never graded by a number) and decided at the energy-model question, when the exposure's Pearson correlation with the declared total-energy column is 0.3 or more in absolute value; below 0.3 it is not raised. The choice of energy model (substitution at fixed energy versus addition) changes what the coefficient means at any r; the 0.3 cut decides only whether the app surfaces it, and is borrowed from the recognizer's rule for when values corroborate a nutrient.
source_note: BLUEPRINT.md §14 rule 1 (lines 547-549) exists but says a nutrient's values 'rise with total energy by a meaningful effect (r >= 0.3, not merely p < alpha)' as evidence for 'High' recognizer confidence that a column is a nutrient -- not a threshold for when the energy model changes the estimand; materiality.py:104 repurposes it. SURFACING_POLICY.md §2.1 (lines 257-260) is an internal ruling with a methods reason: when an alternative changes what Q is (substitution versus addition), M is undefined and the item is Decide regardless -- this supports the 'act on it' grading and routing, not the 0.3 gate. No literature cited for the cut.
note: Code (materiality.py:648-674) matches the mechanics: fires only with lens 'dietary', an energy column and an exposure, |r| >= ENERGY_R = 0.3, changes_question -> band 2, question 'energy_adjustment'. The test pins one fixture (r = 0.64) and would pass with any cut between 0 and 0.64; no test exercises r below 0.3. The meaning-change is a definitional fact about the two energy models; the 0.3 surfacing gate is a convention and should be presented as such (or the noticing raised at any r when an energy column and an exposure are both present).

source_note: MODELING_SEQUENCE.md §0 ruling 2 (line 50-55) exists and says it: 'Exposure quintiles under inference rank lower; they are not blocked. They estimate a coarser contrast, not a false number, and they are the field's primary-analysis convention'; reasoning and sources are in docs/turbotab-next/audit/modeling-sequence-review.json (row '§4 Categories as the analysis model'). NUTRITION_PACK.md:776 says '[CONVENTION, now near-default; quintiles remain expected alongside]'. Verified via Europe PMC: Turner et al. Epidemiol Perspect Innov 2010;7:9 found categorisation in 86% of 58 articles (supports 'customary', not soundness); Bennette & Vickers BMC Med Res Methodol 2012;12:21 'The use of quantiles is often inadequate' (supports 'weaker'). 'Coarser contrast, not a false number' and 'not blocked' are the orchestrator's ruling, a decision with stated methods reasoning, not a published rule.
note: Code matches: methods/exposure_form.py quintiles rung 'rank_lower' under inference, spline 'recommended', linear 'available'; exposure order spline, linear, quintiles, categories, optimal; confounder order spline, linear, categories, quintiles, optimal; only 'optimal' is block_and_record. The information-loss and step-assumption facts are sourced (Bennette & Vickers), but the ranking rule ('rank lower, never block') is a ruling; tests only pin the rung strings, which is appropriate for a convention. Show it as the app's ruling with its sources visible.

source_note: BLUEPRINT.md §11.3 (line 396) exists but is the general leash principle (refuse / block and record / rank and state, scaled by stakes); it says nothing about strata, PSUs or interval width, so it gives a decision rule, not a methods reason. No survey-methods source is cited for 'too narrow'. Standard design-based theory runs the other way for this branch: with PSUs named, dropping the strata usually makes the with-replacement variance larger (conservative), not narrower; 'too narrow where people were sampled in clusters' is the reason for the missing-PSU branch, and survey.py:_names_its_units reuses one tail for both.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_wp10_survey_design.py::test_partial_designs_are_attested_and_a_persons_rows_stay_one_unit (exercises the weights-only branch: no strata and no PSU; it checks the block and attestation, not interval width, and never exercises PSU-without-strata)
note: The statement accurately describes the app: survey.py:408-422 raises Refusal('partial_design') when strata is missing, with the text 'the intervals would treat the PSUs as unstratified, and where people were sampled in clusters they are too narrow', and an attest exit 'My table has no such column; record that'. But the stated reason does not follow for missing strata. After attestation, models/survey.py:build_design (lines 153-160) puts every row in one stratum and keys PSUs by their raw code, so NHANES-style SDMVPSU codes 1/2 reused across strata collapse into two PSUs (df = 1), an interval that is badly mis-specified in either direction. The block itself is defensible as 'name the strata if they exist'; the wording and the post-attestation design need the orchestrator.

source_note: models/effects.py:88 PH_ALPHA = 0.05 carries only the comment 'at the customary level'; no source for the threshold. GRAMBSCH_THERNEAU (Biometrika 1994;81:515) is cited for the test itself (cox.zph's score test), not for 0.05 or for testing the exposure's term only. MODELING_SEQUENCE.md §1 row 11 (line 142) says only 'Diagnostics are reported (proportional hazards by Schoenfeld; residuals and influence)' with no threshold or term rule. So the method is sourced; the decision rule is an unsourced convention.
note: Code matches: stages/effects.py:_ph groups the exposure's columns into one term (self.key), compares each exposure term to effects.PH_ALPHA = 0.05, ignores the global test and covariates for 'failed', and attaches respond_diagnostic exits (all actions if the exposure is one column, else keep_labeled only). The R test is a real check of the chi-square and p against cox.zph to 1e-6, but for the rule it only asserts one simulated non-PH x1 has p < 0.05; it would pass at many other cut-offs. The rule conflicts with the fit stage: models/survival.py:60 PH_ALPHA = 0.01 split over the columns (p < 0.01/P) for its concern, so the same model can be flagged in one place and not the other. The reading already says 'customary'; present it as a convention, and reconcile the two thresholds.

corrected_statement: With a log (an energy-adjustment log_transform on a component) or a nonlinear form (spline or categories) of the donor or recipient, moving k kcal no longer has one effect per kcal: each person's effect depends on k and their own intake, so each point of the substitution curve is the (survey-weighted, where weights apply) average of those effects over the rows on support at that k -- the rows whose shifted intakes stay within the observed range, which shrink as k grows -- not a coefficient difference. With a logged component the label adds that an all-components contrast is not defined.
source_note: MODELING_SEQUENCE.md §2 'Corrected' (lines 205-210) says exactly this and withdraws draft 1's 'ratio rather than difference'. The reasoning is in docs/turbotab-next/audit/modeling-sequence-review.json (lines 583, 798): the curve moves k kcal through the fitted pipeline so it stays a kcal difference whose row-level effects are heterogeneous, and the all-components contrast needs every component on one additive scale, citing Tomova, Gilthorpe & Tennant 2022 AJCN (substitution models perform well 'provided all variables were measured in the same units'). That is an internal ruling with a methods reason, consistent with the cited source; the Tomova quote was not re-fetched here.
note: The heterogeneity is elementary: a term b*log(d) moved to b*log(d - k/c) changes by b*log(1 - k/(c*d)), which depends on d and k; likewise for any nonlinear basis. methods/substitution.py:substitution_curve averages the change in prediction over on-support rows per k (with weights), so the label is true of the computation. The tests compare label strings only (form_8), and test_substitution.py checks the linear-model case by hand but never a logged or spline component, so nothing checks the averaging under a nonlinear form. Outside this claim: substitution_curve_label returns None for linear forms even when the model is logistic and the curve is on the probability scale, where per-person effects also vary with intake.

corrected_statement: When the lens includes neither clinical nor dietary and is not empty (metabolomics, genomics, survey, and also 'other' -- 'Something else, or not sure'), a yes/no outcome with no numeric column whose name reads as a follow-up time is read by default as a status at sampling, counted over one period for everyone (a binary model); the follow-up question is skipped as a stated skip that the user can reopen with 'Ask me anyway'. The rule rests on the lens and on column names, not on the data.
source_note: No methods source. The only rationale is the code comment at estimand.py:176-182 ('Under an assay or survey lens alone a yes/no outcome is a status at sampling (a case or a control, an answer)') and crosswalk default:follow_up_one_period (crosswalk.json:4997, objective Confirm, lenses metabolomics/genomics/survey). That is a decision with a one-line reason, not a sourced rule.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_routing_gate_repair.py::test_4_linked_mortality_asks_the_follow_up_and_fits_cox (pins asked/skipped per lens; does not test 'other' or whether the binary reading is right)
note: Ran follow_up_gate directly (venv/bin/python): lens ['other'] returns 'skipped', the same as ['survey']; [] and ['clinical'] return None (asked). The comment at estimand.py:176-178 says '"something else, or not sure" (no lens): their yes/no outcome is always asked', but follow_up_asked_always only checks for an empty list, so the stored 'other' lens skips -- the code contradicts its own stated rule, and the crosswalk omits 'other'. Also, survey data with linked outcomes (NHANES linked mortality) can be events over follow-up; under the survey lens it is caught only if a column name reads as follow-up (reads_as_follow_up). The default is reversible ('Ask me anyway'), so it is a soft default, but present it as a lens-based convention.

source_note: NUTRITION_PACK.md §01 (lines 28-38, '[SETTLED as a diagnostic]') gives the Atwater reconstruction E_hat = 4P + 4C + 9F + 7A and the ratio table: 0.90-1.10 kcal and grams (pass), ~4.18 kJ, ~0.239 inverse. It is a methods reason (an identity), though the pack itself cites no primary source for the 0.90-1.10 band. The 5% band around 4.184 is nutrition._reconstruct's (nutrition.py: abs(median - KJ_RATIO)/KJ_RATIO < 0.05), and the N-day ambiguity is plain arithmetic recorded after the fifth gate (4 x 1.00 = 4.00 is 4.4% from 4.184).

note: Code matches: readings.unit_day_candidates (kcal x1 within 0.90-1.10; kJ x N, N=1..31, and kcal x N, N=2..31, within 5%) and atwater_unit settles only when the candidates are exactly [('kcal', 1)], with the days left to the user; a median-ratio spread (mixed units) or non-gram macronutrients settle nothing. The c2 fixtures are known-truth simulations (kJ energy; a 4-day kcal total at ratio ~4.00; a 3-day total), not pinned output, and the 8 energy cases pass (run with venv/bin/python; .venv lacks pydantic). source_note: NUTRITION_PACK.md §08 (table row line 896 and text lines 914-920) states this claim nearly word for word; it is an internal ruling with reasons. Verified via Europe PMC: Glymour et al. Am J Epidemiol 2005;162:267-278 (PMID 15987729), 'in many plausible situations, baseline adjustment induces a spurious statistical association' in analyses of change, and 'change-score analyses without baseline adjustment provide unbiased causal effect estimates when baseline-adjusted estimates are biased' -- this supports the change-since-baseline half. Schisterman, Cole & Platt Epidemiology 2009;20:488 defines overadjustment bias for intermediates, which supports the mediator concern. Neither source addresses a baseline level of the outcome's kind beside an incident event, where adjusting for it (or excluding prevalent cases) is the common practice; that half is the pack's own reasoning ('before the outcome, no consequence of it, and it can predict it').
note: Code matches: covariate_guesses.guess (lines ~405-425), when the covariate is in the outcome's class and group and p.followed, returns the class's TIMING_UNKNOWN answers (unknown, yes, unknown) with the reason 'declared without it and, beside, with it', and cites Glymour only when the outcome is not an event; routing_leash.py:99-105 declares the same relation. The test drives a simulated incident cohort but asserts only that the pair is offered and the sentence reads as written; nothing checks which model is less biased on known truth. The pair is reasonable when timing is unknown, but it makes 'without' primary for incident outcomes, where the field usually adjusts for the baseline precursor; show it as the app's ruling with its sources.

source_note: Hanley & McNeil, Radiology 1982;143:29-36 (PMID 7063747) exists and gives the AUC standard error; seal._auc_halfwidth reproduces it exactly: Q1 = A/(2-A), Q2 = 2A^2/(1+A), Var = [A(1-A) + (n1-1)(Q1-A^2) + (n0-1)(Q2-A^2)]/(n1*n0). The assumed AUC of 0.75 is a planning convention (seal.py comment: 'a plan comes before any fit'), not from the source. The macro-F1 rule (1.96*sqrt(0.25/k) on the rarest class) has no source: macro-F1 is not a proportion of the rarest class's rows, so the worst-case binomial interval is an ad hoc stand-in. PRECISION_NOTE (seal.py:616-619) states both as approximations.
test_judged: none found: no test exercises seal._auc_halfwidth or the multiclass branch of seal.measure (test_seal.py only calls measure('regression', n))
note: Code (seal.py:689-731) matches the statement. Nuance: in the binary branch the 'events' passed to Hanley-McNeil are the rarer class (k[0]), not necessarily the event level, and the formula is asymmetric in n1 and n0; the effect on the width is small. The AUC half alone would be 'sourced' (formula from the cited paper, with a stated 0.75 assumption), and the formula is easy to certify with a hand-coded check; the macro-F1 half is a convention and should read as a rough guide ('about'), which the UI already does. The ordinal branch claims no width, as stated.

source_note: models/metrics.py docstring (lines 13-33) gives the definition R2_CV = 1 - SS_res / sum_k sum_{i in k} (y_i - ybar_{-k})^2 and cites Hawinkel, Waegeman & Maere (Am Stat 2024; arXiv:2302.05131). Verified on arXiv HTML: 'The pooling R^2 is an unbiased estimator of the true R^2', 'the pooling estimator should be preferred to averaging estimators', 'The averaging R^2 with test MST estimator is very variable and dramatically downward biased for smaller sample sizes'; their null model predicts the observed (training) mean for out-of-sample rows. Their MST uses an (n+1)/n-inflated variance rather than per-fold training means, a close variant of the app's denominator. Staerk et al. 2024 is quoted for the training-mean definition (not re-fetched). Audit MA-09 is the internal origin.
note: The test is a known-truth simulation (OLS, p = 5, population R^2 0.20, 500 replicates) against an analytic out-of-sample target (0.1345), and also shows that the per-fold test-mean average misses by more than 0.05, so it would fail if the app averaged per fold against test means. Code: modeling.py:1992 sets the reference to the training rows' mean, and the holdout score at :2066-2067 uses it; voice.py:1209-1211 states it (regression only, suppressed under inference). Conflict to resolve in the docs: BEATS_PREDICT.md §17 ruling 7 (line 1494) says the opened cycle's R^2 is 'computed against the cycle's own mean (0.18)', which contradicts both this sentence and the code (test_modeling.py:213 pins the training mean).

source_note: The cited 'lockbox constitution §04' is docs/turbotab-next/reference/LOCKBOX_CONSTITUTION.md §04 (lines 105-128): the eligibility question is asked 'with the target's distribution withheld, because an eligibility criterion comes from the research question and not from the histogram. A rule on the outcome's own range is refused: selecting on the outcome biases the estimates ... that is data-driven cohort selection, which is its own publishable bias.' It is an internal ruling with a methods reason (selection on the outcome) and cites TRIPOD+AI only for eligibility as a participant-flow item; no primary methods source for the bias itself, which is textbook selection-on-the-dependent-variable.
note: Code: content.py:817-843 (one-liner; custom option 'never the outcome'), coach.py:27-28 (no exclusions note describes the outcome), and decisions.py:3797-3915 (_exclusions_leave_the_outcome_alone refuses any rule that reads an outcome column, including a time-to-event outcome's follow-up time and a Goldberg screen's inputs, under every purpose). The test uses a known truth: true fiber slope -0.25 is recovered on the full table by hand-coded NumPy least squares, while the bmi 18.5-30 rule on a bmi outcome biases it by more than 0.1; then it checks the 409 refusal. That certifies the 'never on the outcome' half. The withholding of the outcome's histogram at that question is a design rule that follows from it; no test checks the screen's content.

corrected_statement: The engine says, for every explanation, that SHAP values and accumulated local effects describe a fitted model's predictions, not what changing an intake would do, and refuses to report one as an effect (models/explain.py EFFECT_SAYS; explanation_is_not_an_effect). It sums SHAP over the model-matrix columns made from one input (a category's indicators, a spline's basis) and reports stability as the mean Spearman correlation of importances across bootstrap refits, with no threshold. The plain-group credit split between correlated inputs ('how it splits within a group is arbitrary') and the rule 'one input's share is unstable when the reseeds' rank correlation is under 0.7' are in the BEATS_PREDICT design (R3 Why?, §6 item 6), not yet in the engine.
source_note: Molnar et al. 'General pitfalls of model-agnostic interpretation methods' (arXiv:2007.04131; xxAI 2022): abstract names 'making unjustified causal interpretations' and 'ignoring feature dependencies' as pitfalls, which supports the not-an-effect and correlated-credit points in general. Lundberg & Lee 2017 and Apley & Zhu 2020 are the method sources (SHAP, ALE), not sources for the caveats. The 0.7 rank-correlation threshold has no source anywhere in the repo (BEATS_PREDICT.md line 1067 states it as a rule only).
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_explain.py::test_5a_every_explanation_says_it_describes_the_model_not_an_effect (text shown); no test for the 0.7 rule, which is unimplemented; ::test_1f_stability_over_five_reseeds_is_spearman_of_the_reported_importances checks the rho computation only
note: The first sentence (explanations are not effects) is sourced and shown in the engine. The 0.7 cut is an unsourced convention in a design doc, and the implemented 'grouped' SHAP is grouping by source input, not the correlated plain groups (diet, body size) the beat describes. If the beat ships, the threshold should read as a convention, and the 'arbitrary split' line should be tied to an actual within-group correlation check (§6 item 6's 'summed shares exceed twice its net').
